In the game of Lights Out, pressing a button on the grid triggers a light-up effect that spreads in all directions. The maximum click difficulty arises when trying to turn on every light with the fewest number of clicks. Research has shown that for square grids, this difficulty is at most four times the grid size. Our study aims to improve upon this result by providing a more precise upper limit, specifically log_2(4/3) times the grid side length plus four, which is less than the previous estimate of four times the grid side length.

Image segmentation is a widely used technique in image processing, with numerous applications. The research presented in this paper proposes a novel segmentation model, combining the strengths of the Mumford-Shah model and the Rudin-Osher model. The proposed model addresses the limitations of the Mumford-Shah model, which has a difficult energy function, by incorporating the smoothness constraint from the Rudin-Osher model. The model's convergence is proven and its results are demonstrated through numerical experiments.

The Abstract Interpretation framework has been widely used for program analysis, and its fundamental concept involves a decoupling of the actual and approximate execution of a program. This paper offers a distinct interpretation of this decoupling, separating the approximation processes of the upward phase and downward phase. This new understanding leads to the formulation of the decision problem for optimal approximation, and the proof that the upward phase approximation must be at least as precise as the downward phase approximation to achieve optimality. This paper also provides a distinct characterization of the optimal approximation functions in terms of the lattice's upward and downward functions.

A novel class of phonons called topological phonons has been discovered in materials that combine oscillating sound waves with distinct surface sound waves referred to as "STSs." These phonons, with their distinct properties, have the potential to significantly contribute to the development of oxide ceramics, which are widely used in various applications. In this research, scientists have successfully demonstrated the creation of a material where topological phonons can be controlled using light, which triggers changes in the material's vibrational properties, resulting in enhanced production of specific "Wen phonons." This research provides a new pathway for controlling sound waves in materials and opens up new possibilities for the development of advanced acoustic devices.

An efficient and accurate outlier detection approach in metric spaces is presented. The proposed Rapid and Accurate outlier detection with Proximity Graphs (RAPGP) algorithm leverages a sparse approximation of the nearest neighbor graph to identify outliers within complex datasets. By combining this search structure with distance metrics, the proposed algorithm achieves fast and reliable outlier detection. The proposed RAPGP algorithm is backed by theoretical analysis, supported by comprehensive experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that RAPGP outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, yielding superior accuracy and efficiency. The proposed algorithm is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashishkumar1998/RAPGP.

The radial motion of a slender mirror along the z-axis is analyzed in this context, with its flat surface perpendicular to the axis, centered at a point and oscillating at specific frequencies and amplitudes. As the mirror moves, an observer positioned on the z-axis perceives an atom placed behind the mirror as having a shifted energy structure, appearing as if the atom were located at the mirror's effective position, with its energy levels modified by a z-dependent term. Additionally, an moving atom emits radiation that a stationary observer can detect, with its emission spectrum exhibiting distinct patterns.

When training predictive models on graphs, the behavior of graphs' subgroups can be
evaluated by comparing their outcomes. Our work introduces an approach to ensure
equity among graph subgroups based on the concept of fairness within local groups.
We develop a metric to measure this subgroup fairness and establish a mathematical
definition for locally fair graphs. Our analysis shows that this fairness definition
contrasts sharply with traditional methods used for predicting outcomes on plain data.
To address this, we propose an algorithm that identifies the most equitable graph by
optimizing a specific fairness metric. Our experiments on artificial and real-world
data demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in identifying fair graphs for
predictive tasks.

This research focuses on solving a reversible enzyme process's kinetic model, represented by a nonlinear algebraic system of two equations with variables $x$ and $y$. The model's parameters, with enzyme concentration as a minor factor, are numerous. Utilizing numerical methods in the Maple software, we demonstrate how to obtain an approximate analytical solution by employing an iterative approach based on a minor influence parameter. Additionally, we show how to use Maple to calculate the maximum reaction velocity and enzyme affinity constants under various conditions, with a specific focus on enzyme concentration effects.

In the context of the Large Hadron Collider, the CMS experiment has analyzed proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The study focuses on using events with missing transverse momentum as a means to search for new physics beyond the Standard Model. The analysis includes the examination of events with one or more high-transverse momentum jets in the absence of leptons. The investigation is based on a dataset of 35.9 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions. The results are compared to the predictions of the Standard Model, and a specific limit on the mass of the lightest superpartner has been established within the framework of simplified models featuring natural and divided supersymmetry. The study has determined a lower bound on the mass of the chargino and the lightest neutralino of 850 GeV.

We introduce a new method to identify and analyze the essence of speculative financial bubbles. By leveraging the experiences of individual traders, we establish a statistical model that allows us to calculate the likelihood of traders recognizing and anticipating the conclusion of ongoing bubbles. This model is grounded in the findings of a survey that assessed the perceptions of professional traders working at a large, publicly-owned fund. The results of the survey are then used to create a predictive model for the cessation of a given bubble, which shows that traders generally acknowledge the existence of a bubble but often underestimate its remaining duration. The new method is applied to several well-documented cases of speculative bubbles, including those that were successfully avoided and failed, as well as a recent speculative bubble that was ultimately burst. The technique is also applied to analyze the perceptions of fund managers at a large, publicly-owned fund and is used to calculate the probability of fund performance decline following the discovery of a bubble.

The path integral formulation of quantum mechanics is a mathematical representation of how quantum systems evolve over time, which can be used to analyze the behavior of these systems. By employing numerical simulations, researchers can calculate the path integrals for complex quantum systems, which are otherwise intractable to solve analytically. This paper outlines a technique for simulating and calculating the path integrals of quantum systems, specifically for systems that are constantly being driven or disturbed. It demonstrates how to use two Markov chain Monte Carlo methods to approximate the path integrals of a quantum harmonic oscillator under external influence. By comparing these simulations with exact analytical solutions, the accuracy of these simulations is verified.

Developing a reliable product recommendation system is essential for the success of e-commerce platforms.  However, users' reviews significantly impact both the purchasing process and customer satisfaction.  To address this challenge, we introduce SIFN, a novel approach that leverages users' reviews through a regression model for more accurate recommendations.  The SIFN framework consists of two main components: a network that classifies review sentiment and another that captures product characteristics using the first sentiment layer, followed by an interactive fusion process.  The effectiveness of our proposed method is demonstrated through experiments on real-world datasets.

Recent interest in machine translation has seen a surge in Arabic research, 
despite challenges posed by code-switching in modern Arabic which hinders performance.
To address this issue, we investigated the potential of data augmentation to 
mitigate the effects of code-switching on Arabic-English machine translation.
We examined various frequency-based lexical substitution methods to replace 
high- and low-frequency words with words of intermediate frequency, 
which we found to be effective in enhancing translation quality through 
evaluations on multiple datasets. These improved results were achieved without 
a corresponding increase in computational costs.
We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of the plane originating from a parabolic fixed point acting in a unipotent manner on a horocycle, cannot be finitarily presented.

We investigate the properties of connectable branes within string theories derived from stringy Schrieffer-Wolff transformations, which encompass string models with generalized lambda deformations and specific conformal field theories. Our findings indicate that in generalized lambda deformations, connectable branes are confined to the W-bundle's zero section. We also present concrete examples of connectable branes in strings from Skyrme models based on the SU(2) and U(1)×SU(2)/O(2) groups. Additionally, we offer a thorough examination of connectable conformal D1-branes in SU(2)/U(1) deformations, which serve as a W-bundle-based string model.

This study demonstrates that the Tets/Hex method outperforms the traditional hexahedral element approach in solving the hexahedral mesh generation problem, showcasing enhanced computational efficiency and capability. Leveraging five processors and a combination of three specialized hexahedral elements, the method successfully processes intricate datasets, such as those with over 58 million vertices and 10 million tetrahedra. Utilizing the TetGen mesh generator and a technique involving the subdivision of tetrahedra into six tetrahedra and five hexes, the method effectively generates high-quality hexahedral meshes, even for complex data sets with numerous features and concavities.

The task of relation extraction involves determining how entities within a text are connected through a specific pre-defined relationship. A key challenge in extracting accurate relationships is the issue of semantic ambiguity, where a single entity has multiple types of relationships. To address this problem, we have developed a joint task of knowledge graph link prediction that aims to create a shared representation of entity relationships. By integrating this joint task into the training process of relation extraction models, we can enhance their ability to capture rich entity-relationship information. We have also proposed a new type of knowledge graph link prediction called the hyperedge link prediction, which allows a single triple to be represented as a group of connected entities. This approach provides an alternative way to model relationships and further improves the performance of relation extraction models, as demonstrated through our experimental results.

This study introduces a method for developing a universal analytical model to predict 
converter delays across various flip-flop converters, such as asynchronous rings, 
asynchronous trees, and mixed synchronizers. We employ the curve fitting toolkit 
in Matlab to achieve this objective. We begin by examining the underlying 
converter structures and their associated delay mechanisms. Next, we outline the 
step-by-step process for creating an analytical delay model. Finally, we illustrate 
this approach using examples, including the analysis of single and multi-stage 
asynchronous reset trees and read-only memory units.

Reinforcement learning agents aim to maximize long-term rewards by selecting optimal actions within a given environment. In numerous practical situations, action spaces are extremely vast, often comprising millions of distinct actions. Consequently, slight variations in actions often result in negligible differences in the agents' future rewards. Our research proposes a framework for model-based reinforcement learning that is capable of handling large action spaces by leveraging coarse continuity in the value function. This allows us to derive a set of sufficient conditions under which the Q-function exhibits continuity, even in cases where the environment itself is not continuous. Furthermore, we develop a method to approximate the optimal Q-function using neural networks, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in solving a navigation task within a high-dimensional environment.

A distinct anatomical feature in the human brain, characterized by a prominent longitudinal fissure separating the two hemispheres, is known as the animacy structure. Research has shown that this structure is not merely a superficial resemblance to the human brain, but rather a profound reflection of the underlying anatomical and functional organization of the brain. In this study, we demonstrate that the animacy structure arises from the complex folding patterns of the brain, and that it is closely associated with the location of critical ventral temporal cortex regions, including the fusiform face area, which is involved in facial recognition. Furthermore, we show that the animacy structure is not merely a passive consequence of the brain's folding patterns, but rather an active component of the brain's underlying anatomical and functional organization, and that it is closely associated with the location of critical ventral temporal cortex regions, including the fusiform face area, which is involved in facial recognition.

In multidimensional electromagnetic and elastodynamic finite element simulations, 
postprocessing involves calculating continuous field quantities from discrete 
results. Although conventional approaches like convolutional arranger filters 
effectively re-arrange these computations, they lack adaptability and may distort 
the field's appearance. In contrast, a novel convex optimization-preserving filter 
is introduced to improve upon this process, offering a more precise and flexible 
re-arrangement of field quantities. The proposed filter surpasses traditional 
methods in terms of accuracy and adaptability, and its implementation is detailed 
for both two and three-dimensional simulations.

Our study utilized the high-energy band (2-100 keV) X-ray data from MAXI J1535-571, observed by Insight-HXMT, to analyze the development of a corona in this Galactic black hole X-ray binary during its 2018 outburst. The analysis revealed that the object went through a standard four-stage outburst pattern, characterized by a transition from a type-C to type-B quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) during the super-soft state, followed by a soft state, a hard state, and finally a mixed state. Notably, the evolution of type-C QPO frequency in this object was unique, displaying an initial increase followed by a decrease, before transitioning to QPO characteristics associated with the soft-state and hard-state states. Furthermore, a strong positive correlation was observed between the evolution of type-C QPO frequency and X-ray flux, with frequency increasing as flux increased. Additionally, a similar trend was found between the evolution of type-C QPO amplitude and X-ray flux, with amplitude increasing as flux increased. These findings support the view that type-C QPOs originate from the boundary of the corona and the inner edge of the accretion disk, with the quasi-periodic modulation resulting from the interaction between these two components.

A key challenge in developing socially autonomous robots is achieving adaptive behavior that aligns with human expectations.  To address this, we introduce an innovative approach, Transfer Empowerment (TE), which enables robots to consistently provide reliable, responsive interactions across various tasks.  We accomplish this by integrating a human preference learning method, the Conditional Computation Tree Game, with TE.  In a shared physical environment, we conduct experiments to assess the effectiveness of our approach, comparing robots that prioritize human preferences with those that do not.  The results demonstrate that the former can reliably engage in dependable, responsive interactions, while the latter often fail to do so.  These findings suggest that the TE approach can be a valuable tool for building socially capable autonomous robots.

A novel machine learning approach is presented for identifying substances
by training simulation models and generating diverse substance samples.
Contrastive learning is used to create substance representations, followed by
a simple neural network for substance identification. This method enables
accurate one-shot identification of substances, even when only a single data
point is available. To validate the technique, we successfully applied it to
distinguish between different chemical mixtures in an experiment simulating
a lab environment. This approach offers potential for automating substance
identification in diverse fields, including chemistry and material science.

A Lie 2-algebra can be understood as the categorification of classical Lie algebra concepts. This note provides a comprehensive overview of Lie 2-algebras by initially deriving the definition from a Lie n-algebra categorification and then exploring its equivalent formulations via Lie 2-algebra definitions. It also delves into the key properties of Lie 2-algebras, including their relationship with strict Lie 2-algebras, their connection to Lie algebras with 2-connections, and their categorification connections. A crucial aspect explored is the equivalence table, which outlines various approaches to Lie 2-algebras, their connections, and limitations. Finally, the text examines the Lie 2-algebra's cohomology, including its definition, key properties, and applications in Lie 2-algebra classification.

We introduce a novel method for identifying local keypoint attributes in image pairs called LoFTR, which produces a list of corresponding features in the image pair. Unlike traditional methods, LoFTR does not rely on keypoint detectors and instead uses a fully detector-free approach. By combining two types of Transformers, LoFTR achieves a balance between a global description and a detailed description of features, which is used to find the most relevant points between the image pair. We tested LoFTR on various datasets, including the Sintel optical flow dataset and the KITTI odometry dataset, and found that it outperforms other methods in terms of both speed and accuracy.

In this study, we examine and address a prevalent issue in solar physics: the underestimation of strong magnetic fields in vertical magnetograms. This phenomenon is known as the saturation effect, which occurs when measuring magnetic fields at the solar surface. The problem arises from a common method of inferring magnetic field measurements from vector magnetograms, which tends to inaccurately represent the strength of magnetic fields. To address this issue, we have developed a novel method for correcting the bias in these measurements. Our approach involves re-calculating the horizontal magnetic field components using the line-of-sight component, which helps to mitigate the saturation effect. By applying this method to two datasets, we have demonstrated that it significantly reduces the bias in these measurements. Our results indicate that the corrected measurements are more accurate and reliable, which has important implications for solar physics research.

A newly developed strategy called Independent Demand Side Control is proposed to empower residential users to manage their energy consumption more efficiently. By utilizing a game-theorety approach, this strategy enables users to optimize their energy usage in real-time while adhering to their energy usage plans. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy in achieving considerable cost savings, up to 20%, for participating households.

In the Rastall theory of modified gravity, we've investigated the influence of a magnetic field on the thermodynamic properties of a charged black string. We've discovered that the presence of the magnetic field results in the reduction of the mass of the black string, and we've shown that its temperature can be negatively impacted. We've further found that the emission of Hawking radiation from the black string is influenced by the magnetic field, and under certain conditions, this radiation can be suppressed. Additionally, the magnetic field has been shown to reduce the surface area of the black string, and we've observed that its entropy can decrease as a result.

We apply functional limit theorems to analyze the spectral distributions on the circle arising from the converging speeds in the mean-square version of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. Furthermore, we provide additional examples illustrating diverse spectral distributions.

The Gaia mission's photometric spectroscopy has the potential to significantly contribute to our understanding of the chemical composition of stars in the galaxy. A new method has been developed to accurately predict the metal content of metal-poor stars using only the narrow spectra captured by Gaia's instrument. This method relies on machine learning and was trained using synthetic spectra generated with the FAST code. It was tested using real data from the Gaia Data Release 3 and was found to be effective across a wide range of temperatures and metal concentrations. It was also validated using synthetic spectra from two different codes and was found to produce similar results. This method was then applied to a sample of stars in the galaxy's bulge and was used to identify unique metallicity patterns associated with two distinct bulge populations. These findings were further supported by high-resolution spectroscopy and suggest that these unique populations originated from different periods of galaxy formation.

The frequency and severity of fires in the world are escalating due to climate change, prompting an urgent need to monitor and forecast fire activity. This trend is particularly noticeable in the Global North, where longer fire seasons are being driven by higher temperatures and prolonged drought conditions. This study leverages data on drought and fire conditions from the past 15 years to create a novel prediction model that can be used to assess and monitor the intensity of future fires. This model, known as the Fire Season Intensity (FSI), is calculated using the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and the European Drought Atlas, and it is then validated using a statistical analysis. The results show that FSI is a reliable indicator of fire activity, and it is capable of predicting future fire behavior. The FSI tool is especially useful for regions with limited data availability, and it can be used to inform fire management and policy-making.

The effectiveness of corpus-based metrics in measuring language complexity is well-established, yet the specific aspects of complexity they capture remains unclear. This study focuses on the type of complexity measured by morphological complexity metrics, examining their relationship with the diversity and uniformity of morphological forms within a language. Our research reveals that some of these metrics correlate with the diversity of morphological forms, while others measure the frequency distribution of these forms. Notably, the results of this study suggest that the choice of validation method is crucial in understanding what these metrics actually measure.

Researchers have recently discovered evidence suggesting that small galaxies within clusters of stars may be smaller and fainter than anticipated. Self-interacting dark matter, a theory, could potentially resolve this "core-cusp problem" by scattering dark matter particles within the centers of dwarf galaxies. We examined the possibility of using large clusters of stars as natural telescopes to magnify these small galaxies. Our analysis revealed that this magnification effect is more prevalent than previously thought, potentially allowing us to observe numerous small galaxies within clusters. Furthermore, self-interacting dark matter models could be constrained by observing the distribution of dark matter in the centers of these small galaxies.

Reducing the size of complex AI models is crucial for their practical application, 
especially on devices with limited resources. This paper focuses on efficiently reducing the size of Markov Decision Process models, which are commonly used in robotics and augmented reality. We introduce two innovative approaches that leverage a separate, smaller AI model to guide the main process. The first method uses this smaller AI model to augment the state space, while the second employs it to identify and ignore irrelevant states. The effectiveness of these approaches is demonstrated through the application of reinforcement learning, resulting in significant model compression with minimal impact on the learned policies. The proposed techniques are validated through a detailed analysis of their performance and are further supported by a comprehensive theoretical framework.

M-estimators offer a versatile approach to robust M-estimation, particularly in the context of independent component analysis for non-Gaussian data, and are particularly effective in handling outliers and data with unknown distributions. In this paper, we present the first finite sample convergence results for robust M-estimators in the RAPID ICA framework, and demonstrate their applicability to diverse scenarios, including those involving contaminated data and data with unknown distributions.

Social media posts describing traffic incidents provide a wealth of real-time information, but their unstructured nature poses a significant challenge to automated identification. Geotagged social media posts can be effectively utilized to track traffic incidents, but existing methods struggle to pinpoint their relevance to specific locations and times. This study proposes a novel approach to identify and categorize traffic incidents using geotagged social media data, by leveraging the principles of traffic flow theory and machine learning. The proposed method employs an algorithm to filter incidents occurring within a specific time frame and nearby a particular section of the road network, and evaluates performance through a comprehensive evaluation framework. The results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing methods, with an impressive 93% identification accuracy, and highlights the importance of considering the temporal and spatial spread of traffic incidents.
This study focuses on the solvability of a specific partial differential equation that involves an arbitrary non-standard term on a given domain with an arbitrary boundary condition specified.

In recent years, rare earth metals have been gaining attention due to their unique magnetic properties. However, cobalt and cobalt-based compounds are receiving increased attention due to their potential advantages in magnetic performance. This study utilizes evolutionary exploration to investigate the yttrium-cobalt-boron system, revealing several stable cobalt-rich Y-C-B alloys. These alloys exhibit enhanced cobalt content and can be synthesized using conventional methods, thus reducing rare earth metal usage and improving magnetic performance. The resulting alloys demonstrate promising magnetic properties, with examples including a high saturation magnetization and room-temperature magnetization reversibility.

This study investigates how to optimize risk-sensitive bidding strategies for a display advertising seller participating in multiple auctions simultaneously, while adhering to budget constraints. We examine two distinct risk metrics - Conditional Value at Risk and a newly introduced H-robust risk metric - and develop corresponding bidding algorithms for each that guarantee near-optimal risk minimization under limited budgets. Our results demonstrate that by adapting an existing budget-bidding framework, we can derive efficient solutions that achieve close to optimal risk reduction in scenarios where the advertiser's risk preferences and auction conditions are unknown.

Researchers investigating quantum effects in gravity have proposed a theory that quantum systems' coherence is impeded by the presence of a massive object. The idea is that the system's non-classical characteristics are linked to Wigner negativity, a characteristic of quantum states. However, we argue that this condition is overly restrictive. We demonstrate through counterexamples that there can be quantum systems whose gravitational fields are not classical, yet do not exhibit Wigner positivity. Furthermore, we outline the conditions under which the Wigner negativity can indeed lead to the gravitational field becoming non-classical.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) systems are susceptible to attacks on imperfect random number generators (RNGs), specifically those targeting weak or biased random numbers.  We introduce a quantum block-based privacy enhancement method to counter these vulnerabilities in BBS-QKD systems, where each block undergoes a separate key distillation process.  This approach allows for the calculation of a secure public key without revealing any individual block's raw key data, achieved through a multi-step verification process.  We experimentally demonstrate our scheme, yielding an estimated 1.5 kbps key rate, and validate its effectiveness in mitigating two specific attacks on imperfect RNGs: individual random number bias and bias concatenation.  Our results demonstrate that this scheme enhances the security and practicality of QKD systems in real-world applications.

This research paper investigates the conditions under which a one-parameter submanifold qualifies as a Bertrand curve within a semi-Riemannian manifold, and we derive novel results showing that a Bertrand curve is indeed a type of quasi-Salkowski curve.

This paper investigates the probability distributions resulting from combining independent Feller diffusions, independent standard normal variables, and independent exponential random variables, and reveals that Feller distributions are closed under these combinations. Building upon existing work, our findings extend to the exponential distributions, offering novel results in mathematical diffusion theory. Our research has significant implications for Feller diffusion trees, a concept that we will explore in a separate study linked to financial derivatives, and to financial futures and forwards, whose pricing follows Feller diffusion distributions. We also establish that Feller diffusion distributions are stable under sampling, a property that is relevant to Feller diffusion trees. Our results are supported by novel combinatorial methods and mathematical identities.

We present an innovative diagrammatic technique for analyzing scattering processes of complex, multi-photon quantum states from a two-level quantum emitter confined within a planar waveguide. Our method enables a straightforward representation of scattering amplitudes through a set of basic building blocks and graphical elements, which can be seen as a combination of the underlying emitter's properties and characteristics of the input photon state. When this formalism is applied to various multi-photon scattering scenarios, we observe that our approach provides insights and predictions that surpass those derived from traditional methods, such as diagrammatic multi-photon quantum hydrodynamics.

In the context of the Standard Model of Cosmic Fluid, we've incorporated the Dirac fermion field into the standard model of cosmology. Our work focuses on the dark energy's influence on the large-scale structure of the universe, specifically examining how spin-dependent parameters impact cosmic evolution. The dark energy model we're investigating has the property of boosting, and our analysis reveals that the spin-dependent parameters significantly influence the universe's expansion and the formation of large-scale structures. The case of scalar dark energy serves as a baseline for comparison, and our findings suggest that the spin-dependent parameters can be constrained by the weak lensing data and the cosmic microwave background, potentially leading to significant deviations from the predictions made by the standard model of cosmology.

We'll examine Faulhaber's observation that the sum of the r-th powers of the first
n natural numbers forms a polynomial in n of degree r+1, with its coefficients
including the Bernoulli numbers. This discovery is attributed to Johann Faulhaber,
a 17th-century German mathematician. Later, Leonhard Euler developed formulas for
these coefficients and discovered a notable property of the Bernoulli numbers.

This paper presents a novel differential Continuous Phase Modulation (DCPM) detection method that enhances enhancement delay without compromising the robustness against phase noise. Unlike current proposals, which often suffer from reduced reliability due to increased detection complexity, the proposed approach maintains a significant robustness advantage. By leveraging a non-coherent detection scheme, the proposed delay enhancement is achieved without increasing the receiver complexity. We specifically focus on Offset CPM, a subclass of DCPM, and provide an in-depth analysis of the detection method's performance, including its phase noise and distortion robustness. Furthermore, the proposed delay enhancement technique is experimentally evaluated through Monte Carlo simulations, which demonstrate the receiver's resilience against both phase noise and distortion.

A key challenge in training reward models for reward-based reinforcement learning is the labor-intensive process of manually labeling data.  We address this issue by proposing a cluster-based approach that uses human feedback to label reward models, thereby reducing the need for extensive manual labeling.  This method involves dividing tasks into clusters based on visual features and asking humans to rank these clusters, which is more efficient than ranking individual tasks.  We introduce two visual clustering methods - using frame-level video content and game content - to facilitate clustering and ranking.  We then utilize these human rankings to train reward models, which we demonstrate through experiments on the Big Visions Benchmark and the Mini World Benchmark, where our approach outperforms previous methods that rely on hand-crafted features and human labels.

This study examines the impact of noncommutative geometry on the internal structure of the nucleon. By utilizing configuration space wave functions derived from the SU(6) shell model, we investigate how noncommutativity affects the proton's radial distribution. The wave function's radial part is expanded in terms of the deformation parameter $\theta$, revealing the influence of noncommutative geometry on nucleon structure.

In a toric code with frustration patterns on a planar lattice, topological edge modes arise due to long-range frustration connections. The number of these modes is determined by the minimum count of frustrated edges meeting specific parity conditions, which can be formulated as a matrix problem. For a triococoon lattice, two types of topological edge modes are found, each exhibiting distinct properties. One mode features no frustration along the edges, while the other has no frustration in the interior. Both modes share the same topological index but have different patterns of frustration along the edges.

We examine the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of complex Hermitian random band matrices with limited rank perturbations, where a submatrix of size $M$ within a larger matrix of size $N$ holds the key information. Our findings confirm that under the given conditions, the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of these perturbed band matrices exhibit the same statistical properties as those predicted by a specific theoretical model involving two parameters, $\lambda$ and $\kappa$. Furthermore, this model accurately describes the same properties in other types of complex random matrices, such as the Dyson Brownian motion. As a consequence, we derive a formula that calculates the transition probabilities between different types of matrix spectra, specifically between band-like and bulk cases.

Recent advancements in conversational understanding have been heavily reliant
on the success of general language pre-training techniques. Nevertheless,
recent findings indicate that these techniques have reached a plateau in
conversational settings, and we argue that incorporating semantic context is
essential for effective conversational AI. As a result, we propose a new
pre-training method called MEAN (Meaning-based Pre-training), which uses
real-world semantic resources to improve the quality of conversational AI.
Our pre-training model is based on semantic networks and incorporates a
novel resource that maps words to their corresponding semantic categories.
Our experiments demonstrate that our pre-training method significantly
outperforms existing techniques across multiple conversational tasks, and
our analysis reveals that incorporating semantic context is crucial for
conversational AI.

The rise of machine learning has brought with it a significant challenge: understanding the complex algorithms that power these models. This issue, known as the explainability problem, is critical to the development of trustworthy AI systems. This study aims to set the stage for future breakthroughs in algorithmic interpretability by establishing a foundational framework. This framework is grounded in cognitive science, aiming to explain how humans learn and grasp new concepts. It also introduces the concept of cognitive intricacy, a metric that quantifies the level of difficulty in understanding an algorithm. This framework provides a structured approach to explainability, including a taxonomy of explainable models, principles for interpretability, and a set of guiding principles. By doing so, it lays the groundwork for future breakthroughs in machine explainability.

An unsupervised algorithm called the Random Forest of Isolation Trees, or iForest, is highly regarded for detecting anomalies in data. It is an extension of the Isolation Tree concept, which is a decision tree-based method that splits data into isolated clusters. Unlike traditional decision trees, the isolation tree doesn't require labels and is particularly suited for anomaly detection tasks. The iForest method combines multiple isolation trees to create an anomaly score for each data point, with lower scores indicating higher anomaly likelihood. The iForest method is computationally efficient and scales well to large datasets. However, the iForest method has a drawback in that it's sensitive to the order of the data, which can lead to inconsistent results. To address this limitation, a new variant of the iForest method, called TiWS-iForest, has been developed. The TiWS-iForest method is a lightweight, efficient anomaly detection method that is based on the iForest algorithm and is designed to operate within the constraints of small devices and edge computing environments. The TiWS-iForest method is a Anomaly Scoring System that is able to run on devices with limited resources and is particularly suited to scenarios where data is weakly guided. The TiWS-iForest method is a breakthrough in the field of anomaly detection and is expected to have a significant impact on the way we detect and prevent anomalies in data.

A novel method for Bayesian extreme value analysis is introduced, focusing on modeling the arrival of extreme events as a Poisson process. This approach parameterizes the extreme value distribution in terms of the underlying Poisson process's intensity, yielding time-based parameters that are easier to interpret. The result is a more stable estimation process, which is particularly beneficial when dealing with events defined by specific thresholds. The reliability of this method is demonstrated through numerical simulations and a practical application involving the analysis of daily rainfall in London.

The concept of an ideal average cross section was initially proposed by B. Cabos in 1979. Building on this, researchers have sought to identify specific regions within the context of multi-parton interactions that achieve this cross section on a parton-by-parton basis. Our analysis reveals areas where the cross section remains stationary for four-parton and five-parton final states. A four-parton area was previously identified by one of our co-authors, and we now extend this finding to encompass the aforementioned four and five-parton areas. Furthermore, we propose a general formalism applicable to any final state and calculate the corresponding four-parton areas for all multi-parton final states up to eight-parton states.

This study presents COMET-ATOMIC 2020, the 12th edition of the task, which involves evaluating a knowledge graph's coverage of common sense using the ATOMIC network. Participants were tasked with identifying a subset of key concepts within the ATOMIC network and constructing a new knowledge graph based on their input.

The Hi-GAL survey's data processing workflow is outlined in this document, which leverages the Herschel archive through the ARCES pipeline to generate reduced datasets. Hi-GAL's sensitivity to molecular gas in the Galactic plane necessitates the development of sophisticated tools to manage the data's complexity. Hi-GAL's unique capabilities in detecting molecular gas and protostars are highlighted, with a detailed description of its scientific goals provided. Hi-GAL's reduction pipeline's performance in creating maps and source catalogues is presented, including a discussion of the survey's sources, which are further analyzed in subsequent stages. Hi-GAL's data availability and associated catalogues are detailed, with a focus on the survey's scientific goals.

The globular cluster NGC 2808, which contains a complex blend of stars, has been the subject of a recent study that aimed to determine if there were any differences in metal content between its various star populations. Using the HARPS-N spectrograph, researchers obtained high-resolution spectra of 15 blue stars with low metal content and 15 blue stars with high metal content. By analyzing these stars, they found that the lower metal content group had average iron and oxygen levels of [Fe/H] = -2.11 and [O/Fe] = 0.00, while the higher metal content group had [Fe/H] = -1.79 and [O/Fe] = 0.10. This confirmed that there were different levels of metal content in the cluster's blue stars.

In a single file diffusion process, particles are confined to a one-dimensional channel and cannot pass each other. Researchers have discovered a long tail in the distribution of exit times, which can be reinterpreted through an alternative model where it's modeled as the duration of exit events. A study of this duration, which has not been explored before, reveals a similar long tail behavior. Upon closer examination, it's found that the median exit time is proportional to the square of the number of particles, which aligns with initial conditions. Further analysis has revealed that the distribution of exit times and the duration of exit events exhibit power-law behaviors, which can be attributed to a combination of mechanical and entropic factors.

Quantum mechanics' noncommutative property poses challenges to traditional interpretations of the quantum Bayes' theorem, highlighting the significance of the Lüders rule for maintaining the consistency of the theorem. Utilizing Lüders rule, we demonstrate that quantum mechanics resolves the paradoxical loop hole identified in prior studies, thereby affirming the quantum representation of Bayes' theorem through noncommutative operator algebra. Furthermore, we illustrate an experimental setup that validates the consistency of the theorem, thereby providing a quantum framework for understanding Bayes' theorem, alongside an examination of its potential applications in quantum information processing.

We introduce a novel concept for calculating the energy density of a system composed of $N$ particles, where $N$ can be as low as 2, and is confined within a finite volume $V$. This system is subject to the strong interaction and temperature. Our approach utilizes lattice QCD to compute the energy density, and we present numerical results for the case of $N=2$, and quark systems with two flavors, and calculate the corresponding temperature dependence of the equation of state. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of a quark chemical potential on the system and examine its effect on the phase diagram.

In this paper, we focus on the mod-$p$ Steenrod algebra $\mathcal{A}_p$ for a prime number $p \geq 3$, and its cohomology group for the $\mathbb{F}_p$-coefficient of the mod-$p^2$ Steenrod algebra. We identify specific, non-ignorable components in the mod-$p^2$ Steenrod algebra's cohomology group, deriving the modular $p^2$ relations for $p \geq 3$.

A new photometric technique has been developed to measure astronomical objects' brightness across a wide range of wavelengths, from 100 to 300 nanometers. This technique utilizes three special filters, each with distinct properties, to capture data in the ultraviolet spectrum. By employing a camera with a lens that has a short focal ratio, scientists can achieve a fast and efficient data collection rate. Our model demonstrates that this approach can accurately measure the brightness of small objects, such as those with a diameter of 10 centimeters, and is capable of detecting faint signals. Our proposed model, called the Lyman-alpha Filter Model (LAFM), is designed to measure specific wavelengths, including the Lyman-alpha, Lyman-beta, and Lyman-gamma lines, and is particularly useful for studying Lyman-alpha emission. Our results show that LAFM can accurately measure the brightness of small objects, such as those with a diameter of 10 centimeters, and is capable of detecting faint signals. In many distributed control systems, interconnected agents with symmetrical connections can be effectively managed by a specific class of graph filter controllers. This study investigates the optimal parameters for these controllers, setting specific performance goals such as ideal tracking, while focusing on specific network types like undirected networks. It is discovered that, under certain network conditions, the optimal controller parameters can be set as either all the same or unique for each node, contingent upon whether the network includes both parallel and unique relationships. A new method is proposed to identify these optimal parameters, which relies on a more detailed understanding of the network's connectivity and includes calculating the most efficient sampling of nodes in control networks with multiple relationships. This approach is then tested on a network of interconnected vehicles, showing its potential to synchronize their movements.

We introduce a novel technique for automatically organizing dynamic visual content into themed collections, which can be continuously expanded upon by incorporating individual user input. Our approach is rooted in a semantic memory model that enables the creation of interconnected visual associations. We present an algorithm that facilitates this process by employing associative color retrieval and incorporating principles from cognitive psychology. Our findings indicate that this technique outperforms alternative methods in producing more comprehensive and coherent categorizations of unorganized visual content. We showcase the applicability of this method in various practical settings, including analyzing social media platforms.

This paper introduces a novel, secure communication system, referred to as Keyless Verification (KV), which employs channel noise to generate ephemeral authentication keys. A transmitter encodes a message for the receiver, who then verifies its authenticity using an error correction algorithm. The KV protocol is analyzed in the context of the binary additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel. The study derives a theoretical framework for calculating the error probability, considering both retransmission and soft decoding strategies. The results are validated through numerical simulations. The KV protocol is demonstrated to provide enhanced security over traditional methods, albeit at a slight increase in error probability.

We investigate the transport properties of a driven particle with a washboard potential, used to model various systems such as Josephson junctions and nanowires under microwave radiation, as well as nanomechanical resonators subjected to optical tweezers. When a driven particle moves in a dissipative environment, it may experience uniform motion, occurring above specific thresholds of drive strength, which are unique to each potential. We analyze the critical thresholds for three different potentials: the sinusoidal Josephson potential, a simplified model sinusoidal potential, and a customizable asymmetric potential. Our results show that the critical thresholds vary significantly with drive type - in-line with the quasiparticle current in Josephson junctions, or with the displacement in mechanically driven resonators - and are universally higher than previously estimated values.

This study introduces an innovative approach called AdLaP, a versatile extension of Stock and Watson's local projections (LP) method, which can be used to estimate impulse response functions with ease. AdLaP is capable of adjusting the bandwidth of LP in the context of IRF estimation, allowing for more precise estimation. The adaptable selection of the bandwidth in AdLaP is based on the principle of minimizing mean squared error, providing a more efficient estimation. The method's efficacy is illustrated through its application to two well-known data sets.

The Landau gauge charge in the presence of a vacuum of finite radius experiences a non-zero angular Casimir Poincaré momentum due to its interaction with the curvature of the boundary. This boundary curvature generates a non-uniform electromagnetic field that exerts a force on the charge. As the charge moves, it generates its own non-uniform electromagnetic field, which in turn causes torque on the charge, resulting in a unique angular momentum. This unique angular momentum arises from the interplay between the charge and the vacuum's curvature, which can be interpreted as a result of the charge effectively experiencing a different magnetic field due to its interaction with the boundary. This research introduces a novel approach to Named Entity Recognition (NE R) in Refinement Graph Networks (FGNET-RH), which expands upon the integration of refinement graphs in HNNs. We incorporate refinement graphs into FGNETs to create a new framework that enables the incorporation of prior knowledge, which is particularly beneficial for FGNETs in ERL. We then apply the FGNET-RH to enhance the recognition of fine-grained entities in Refinement Hyperbolic Named Entity Classification (RH-NER). We also introduce a new dataset, Fin-Detailed Entity Corpus (FDEC), to support the evaluation of FGNET-RH's performance. The results demonstrate that the proposed FGNET-RH outperforms existing baselines in both synthetic and real-world datasets, with a notable improvement in the performance of RH-NER on FDEC.

The general class of univalent functions $S$ was initially studied by Sternel in 1936, with the constraint that the second Hankel determinant, $|a_2 a_3 - a_1^2|$, is less than one-half. This led to the definition of the class $U$ by Ma and Wu in 1939, with an alternative form of this determinant less than one. We revisit and expand upon these results by providing broader generalizations applicable to any class $S$ with specified constraints on the second Hankel determinant.

In the context of cloud computing, a crucial task is assigning loads to virtual machines. This paper proposes a new approach, called Prepartition, for effectively distributing loads across VMs in large data centers. The Prepartition strategy involves dividing the workload into subtasks and optimally assigning them to VMs to achieve the best possible load distribution. We have mathematically demonstrated the Prepartition strategy's optimality and validated the results through simulations. Furthermore, the Prepartition strategy's scalability has been shown to offer significant advantages over existing approaches, such as Round Robin, by achieving better load distribution and showcasing near-optimal performance.

In many strategic interactions, particularly when multiple agents are involved, predicting outcomes based on their strategies is challenging. The concept of equilibrium, where an agent's strategy is unaffected by others' choices, provides a useful framework for making predictions. The paper proposes a novel approach to learning equilibria through the introduction of the Fixed Point Network (FPN), a neural architecture designed to address the issue of finding points of convergence. The FPN incorporates an inversion layer to compensate for the limitations of standard optimization methods in learning complex equilibria. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments in both simple games and in real-world applications involving human behavior, showcasing its ability to improve predictions.

A novel, non-invasive approach is introduced to establish the maximum potential impact of interventions within complex systems. This impact can be quantified using the do-calculus framework, particularly in scenarios where the Do-Calculus Impact (DICI) is defined as a sum of three distinct terms, two of which are easily computable, while the remaining term is constrained by the maximum possible influence between random variables. By leveraging this constraint, an upper limit on the system's response to unmeasurable interventions can be determined, even in the absence of direct system knowledge. Furthermore, an alternative formulation of DICI is presented, which is particularly advantageous in high-dimensional systems, as it relies on information-theoretic principles to set a system-specific upper limit on the impact of interventions.

This study addresses the issue of covert attacks on linear time-invariant systems with sensor failures, focusing on developing predictive models to anticipate system behavior and detecting ongoing attacks. The researchers developed an attack detection module based on a Kalman filter to identify active assaults and a predictive model to system behavior during an attack. The proposed approach utilizes a sliding window to collect data and estimate model parameters for predicting future system behavior. The study presents analytical expressions for predictive model accuracy under attack and validates the method through simulation tests.

A new extension of GraphEASE, called GAE-ISumm, is introduced to generate abstractive summaries in Indian languages using trained monolingual corpora for each respective language. It expands the original GATree model by incorporating abstract representation learning and monitoring-less abstractive summarization capabilities. Evaluation results demonstrate that GAE-ISumm excels in producing coherent and accurate summaries across multiple Indian languages, surpassing GATree and other state-of-the-art models.

A finite s-ring is a fundamental structure in algebraic topology, composed of a set of subgroups, with the subgroup's closure under subgroup's operation being a subgroup. The s-ring is equipped with an algebraic structure, with a basis defined by the subgroup's idempotent, with the ring's properties being a combination of the subgroup's and s-ring's properties. The s-ring is considered to be of Noether type if its set of idempotents forms a finitely generated module over its ring structure. The s-ring's properties being of Noether type are explored and generalizations of known results for s-ring are established.

A recent hypothesis has suggested that an unseen population of massive stars could be driving the observed acceleration in the proper motions of nearby stars. To evaluate this idea, researchers focused on five stars with notable acceleration signals and found that constraints from published astrometric studies are more stringent than previously thought. Specifically, studies on $\chi^1$ Orionis, $\sigma^1$ Octantis, and the binary system of $\sigma^2$ Velorum reveal that any hidden companions must be either very low mass or very distant. On the other hand, studies on $\mu^1$ Cephei and $\mu^2$ Cephei indicate that hidden companions, if they exist, must have masses less than $10 M_\odot$ and distances greater than $1000$ AU. These findings challenge the idea that a population of massive, dark stars could be responsible for the observed acceleration in the proper motions of these five stars.

Deep learning techniques have become ubiquitous in numerous applications, 
despite their impressive performance, the theoretical underpinnings of these 
methods remain a subject of ongoing research. The Variational Autoencoder, 
a widely studied technique, has been the focus of numerous studies, 
demonstrating that its variational inference process converges under certain 
conditions. However, a key limitation of this approach lies in its reliance on 
computing the inverse of the input data covariance matrix, which is computationally expensive. To overcome this limitation, a new regularization technique has been proposed, transforming the objective function into a form that does not require matrix inversion. To further enhance its efficiency, the objective function has been simplified by relaxing the rank constraint, thereby reducing its complexity. To validate its effectiveness, a numerical experiment was conducted using high-dimensional data, and the results indicate that this approach achieves competitive performance while significantly reducing computational costs.

The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to widespread deployment of IoT-enabled devices in our daily lives, including smart home gadgets, smart city infrastructure, and industrial equipment. IoT gadgets, however, are vulnerable to cyber threats, including hacking and DoS attacks, due to their limited processing capabilities and lack of security features. To address this concern, this research proposes a private blockchain-based solution to safeguard vulnerable IoT devices against cyber attacks. By leveraging blockchain's secure and decentralized nature, the proposed approach enhances the overall security of IoT devices, including those used in smart homes, by implementing a private blockchain network and deploying a DHT-based node placement algorithm to optimize the system's performance.

This paper presents an innovative method for quantizing L-values in an LDPC decoder, utilizing a neural network to establish a mapping between Q-channel soft inputs and L-bit Q-ary quantized L-values. Unlike previous binary or multi-bit soft decoders, which are hindered by low hardware efficiency, this approach utilizes multi-bit decoding with reduced precision to enhance hardware performance. The proposed method employs a multi-layer perceptron neural network to establish a quantization mapping, optimizing the trade-off between hardware efficiency and decoding performance. Furthermore, this approach can be customized for each Q-channel input independently, allowing for improved performance. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through successful decoding of an LDPC code with 64,800 bits at a rate of 0.5 and a code rate of 33/160 under AWGN conditions, utilizing 4-bit quantized L-values.

A static graph's planarity is determined by its ability to be drawn on a 2D plane without any edges intersecting. When this planarity can also be represented in an upward format, where the y-coordinate of a node increases as one follows an edge, the graph is considered to have an upward planar representation. This paper focuses on detecting and constructing an upward planar representation for a given graph, with the addition of a special vertex, 'root', that is chosen as the starting point for the upward representation. The problem of finding such a representation is complex, with the current best-known results involving finding an induced subgraph, with the removal of which results in an upward planar representation. This paper presents a new and improved result, showing that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable with the 'degree' of the chosen 'root', as the parameter. This new result improves upon a previous bound and provides a more efficient algorithm for finding such a representation. The approach involves the use of the 'width' of the graph, as the parameter, and shows that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable with the 'width' of the graph, as the parameter. The reliability of crowdsourced data is compromised by human uncertainty and bias, which can be quantified and mitigated through the use of various methods. By analyzing the distribution of uncertain responses, it's possible to identify patterns that inform the development of more effective data cleaning techniques. This paper proposes a unique approach to address this challenge, leveraging a combination of ensemble modeling and entropic analysis to improve the accuracy of crowdsourced datasets.

We are examining the decay of smooth norms of transfer operators associated with given semiflows. The decay rate of these operators is directly influenced by the growth rate of periodic orbits within the semiflow system.

A novel type of covering array, called the minor strength-2 covering array, is introduced in this paper as a more efficient alternative to traditional pairwise covering arrays. We establish fundamental properties of this new design and determine the minimum size for specific cases. We also introduce an innovative method for constructing minor strength-2 covering arrays and demonstrate its practical applications in creating smaller covering arrays.

This study demonstrates that contests involving nonlocal games with up to two intertwined players and any number of parties can be solved efficiently using a classical computer. The findings extend existing research on contests between two intertwined players with multiple parties, which was previously established as being solvable efficiently. Additionally, the research broadens the existing knowledge by including contests with fewer than fully intertwined parties, which were previously unexplored. The study also provides a detailed, step-by-step explanation of the nonlocal game reduction technique previously developed.

A detailed experiment was conducted to assess the effectiveness of a search algorithm called GEP-CR in automatically replicating software crashes. The CR module within GEP-CR is designed to automatically find inputs that trigger bugs in programs. It uses a unique search strategy that combines an adaptive approach with a guided method to improve its ability to find high-quality inputs that replicate crashes. The CR module has been thoroughly tested on a large set of open-source software applications and has outperformed other existing input search methods in multiple studies. The goal of our experiment was to validate the reliability of GEP-CR's success by replicating it in a different setting. The experiment involved applying GEP-CR to a different set of software applications and comparing the results to the original study. The results showed that the replicated outcomes were consistent with the original findings, thus confirming the effectiveness of the search algorithm. The experiment also revealed that the differences in performance could be attributed to variations in the software characteristics and the type of bugs present in the programs. The findings of the study have important implications for the field of software testing and bug detection, as they demonstrate the importance of using a reliable and effective search strategy to improve the accuracy of bug detection in different settings.

Theoretical models suggest a complex vortex phase diagram in type-II cuprate superconductors, which could explain the observed complex magnetic behavior in these materials. To test these predictions, we conducted magnetoresistance measurements on a single-crystal sample of optimally doped Bi$_2$Sr$_2$Ca$_2$Cu$_3$xO$_{10+\delta}$. Our study reveals a previously unreported square-square transition between two vortex lattice states, which occurs at low temperatures and high magnetic fields. This discovery is supported by scanning SQUID measurements, which reveal the presence of vortex domains in the same sample. Our findings validate theoretical models and open the door for further exploration of the high-field vortex phase diagram in cuprate superconductors.

Our investigation focuses on the thermal emission of photons produced during the initial stages of heavy-ion collisions. We have discovered that the influence of viscosity on this emission is significantly greater than its effect on hadrons. Notably, viscosity modifies the anisotropic flow of photons by approximately ten times more than it does for hadrons. This phenomenon is attributed to the high momentum of photons, which amplifies the impact of viscosity. As a result, we propose that precise measurements of photon anisotropic flow can provide valuable insights into the properties of quark-gluon plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions.

We've developed a comprehensive approach to identify the consistent magnetic configurations in a kagome lattice with uniaxial anisotropy and an external magnetic field. The resulting phase diagram exhibits a wealth of complex structures, including conformal and non-uniform magnetic patterns, as well as a phase that displays local ferromagnetic properties with three out-of-plane spins. Our analysis also reveals a novel phase characterized by the presence of $3_1$-magnetic symmetry.

Large-scale interventions in fields like medicine and marketing often involve multiple interventions and diverse outcomes, which necessitate controlling false discovery rates. However, the intricate relationships between these outcomes can hinder interpretation. To address this, researchers have developed interventions effect identification, which measures the difference between two interventions. Despite this, the standard methods for estimating intervention effects fail when the number of tests is large, which is problematic in fields like marketing where many tests are conducted. To overcome this issue, we propose a new framework for estimating intervention effects under the control of the dependent false discovery rate. This new framework is demonstrated through the analysis of the effects of various advertising interventions on consumer behavior.

Two distinct expansions of an infinite series in ascending powers of a small variable $t$ are analyzed.  The series represents the expansion of distances between celestial bodies, squared, and its value is based on the current year minus 1629.  The validity of the series relies on Kepler's laws and assumes that $t$ is less than $(\frac{2}{3)\pi)$ radians.  The first expansion provides an accurate approximation for the year 1629 and offers a theoretical estimate for future years, albeit with potential inaccuracies.  The second expansion, derived from successive approximations, converges to an exact solution for any given year, provided it is not too far in the future.  This method can be repeated to achieve any desired degree of precision.

The anomaly in the magnetic moment of a muon, as well as the mass difference of W bosons, can be resolved through the interplay between the pseudo-scalar and components of the standard three-family Higgs boson, as part of a type-X two-Higgs-doublet model.

In the rapidly evolving landscape of information retrieval, users increasingly rely on advanced search capabilities to find relevant resources. Despite conventional methods, such as keyword searches, often fall short in meeting users' needs, research into concept discovery has gained momentum in recent years. This concept discovery approach, however, has not been thoroughly explored in the context of information retrieval. To bridge this gap, we propose SWIFTER, a novel framework that leverages crowd-sourced input to derive user intent from ambiguous queries and presents a structured process for extracting these concepts. By combining computational and human intelligence, SWIFTER achieves a high level of accuracy in discovering user concepts, as evidenced by our evaluation results.

This study presents an unsupervised method to calculate the distance between speakers in conversations, which is not based on speaker labels. A novel deep neural network is designed to process raw speech data and generate a distance matrix. The network's architecture is symmetric, and the output is a two-channel sequence model that produces aligned representations for two speakers. A loss function is used to train the network, which minimizes speaker distances within a group and maximizes distances between speakers from different groups. A symmetric regularization term is also added to ensure the network's output is symmetric. The proposed method is evaluated on the TED-LIUM 4 corpus, which contains discussions from conference settings, and achieves results comparable to a supervised approach.

We introduce SSCAP, an unsupervised approach for temporal action segmentation that relies on self-supervised learning. SSCAP's pre-training strategy is based on Language-driven Action Segmentation and Retrieval (LALR), utilizing a rich set of hand-crafted action descriptions to represent video segments. By breaking down these action descriptions into distinct activity phases, SSCAP enables a more detailed and accurate action segmentation process. The method's parameters are then fine-tuned on a large unsupervised video dataset, where a temporal action detection model is trained by maximizing the similarity between activity-phase and pseudo-label parsers. Evaluations on two datasets from the Temporal Action Detection domain, THUMOS18 and Kinetics600, demonstrate that SSCAP achieves state-of-the-art results, with a R@10 of 10.1% on THUMOS18 and a mAP of 36.9% on Kinetics600.

Using the present algebra, we've identified two types of pentaquark states - $P_{5q}$ and $M_{5q}$ - which are composed of a charm-anticharm quark pair and four other quarks. These states, with hidden charm, are a result of the spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking, and we've found two sets of pentaquark bound states - one set with states around 2.2 GeV and the other near 2.5 GeV. These findings are in line with those obtained from other approaches, and we've also made predictions for the states' decays, which are expected to be detectable at the LHCb experiment.

In computer science education, various methods are employed to assess student understanding, with traditional detailed code reviews and bug-fixing exercises being common. An alternative approach is the use of conceptual questions, with different styles including inquiry-based questions, which can be answered with a single word, to gauge a student's ability to identify and rectify flaws in a piece of code. A study involving 120 students and 120 submissions compared the effectiveness of inquiry-based conceptual questions against traditional detailed review and bug-fixing exercises. The results showed that conceptual questions are as effective as their more complex counterparts in detecting and correcting errors, with the added benefits of being quicker to create, easier to administer, and less time-consuming to grade.

Domain adaptation seeks to enhance classification performance by leveraging knowledge from unrelated training data distributions. Recent studies have attempted to overcome limitations of traditional domain adaptation methods by utilizing theory transfer, which involves repurposing high-level conceptual knowledge from the source domain. Theory transfer can be particularly beneficial when there are significant differences between the source and target domains. However, existing theory transfer methods primarily focus on fully-supervised settings and often overlook the inherent noise in theoretical data. To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel semi-supervised theory transfer approach for source-free domain adaptation. This method involves transferring knowledge from high-dimensional feature space to a low-dimensional theoretical space, utilizing a multi-level feature selection approach to minimize noise. Furthermore, this theory space is then utilized to guide the reconstruction of target data distribution, leveraging the proposed semi-supervised representation alignment approach. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on various datasets, including image and point cloud data.

A novel nuclear thermal propulsion system, featuring a remote gas core reactor, has been developed to achieve higher specific impulse values. The system utilizes a space-based rocket configuration, powered by a small-scale reactor weighing around 100 kg, with a 10 cm diameter, to facilitate controlled combustion of a gaseous fuel and a 40:60 helium/hydrogen mixture as a coolant. The use of a 235U fuel pellet in a porous structure enables efficient fuel consumption and enhanced thermal conductivity through the porous structure, allowing for a higher specific impulse value of approximately 900 seconds. The specific impulse can be further increased by adjusting the coolant and fuel ratios, as well as by using a porous fuel structure, while maintaining a high combustion efficiency. The specific power of the system is estimated to be around 1000 kW/kg, and the use of a space-based propulsion system enables higher thrust values, as well as the possibility of achieving higher velocities. The system has been designed to minimize the risk of nuclear accidents, and to ensure safe operation in space, with the use of a space-based reactor configuration.

Machine learning's potential for accurately identifying interaction locations within large astroparticle detectors has been overlooked in recent studies. We've developed an innovative approach that integrates neural networks with a geometric representation of detector structures, enabling the localization of particle interactions. We've created an in-depth, three-dimensional representation of the IceCube neutrino detector and incorporated it into a neural network framework. We've also expanded this to include a more complex network that captures the interactions within. We've tested the efficacy of this method in localizing particle interactions within three distinct scenarios: neutrino interactions, muon creation, and cosmic ray interactions. Our novel domain-informed network achieved exceptional accuracy in these tasks, surpassing traditional fully-connected neural networks by a significant margin. We've observed that increasing the network's capacity can further enhance accuracy, yet this comes with a notable increase in computational demands. We've also examined the potential of our approach for reverse problems, such as inferring neutrino energies and directions. We've discovered that incorporating the neural network's capacity to handle unobserved variables can lead to improved accuracy in reverse problem solutions.

The study of substellar exoplanets and the broader extrasolar environment necessitates the development of comprehensive spectral models that can accurately predict the absorption spectra of various molecules under different atmospheric conditions. To facilitate this, we have developed a database of absorption cross-sections for key molecules found in brown dwarf and exoplanet atmospheres, including H2O, CH4, NH3, and TiO. Our approach involves generating these cross-sections using the Line-by-Line program and then converting them into transmission spectra using the Monte Carlo radiative transfer code, which can be directly compared to the transmission spectra obtained from the James Webb Space Telescope. Our line lists and spectra are accessible through the EXOPLINES website, which also hosts the code used to create these cross-sections, allowing for the line list to be tailored to specific wavelength ranges.

This paper offers a comprehensive overview of the fundamental concepts and theoretical underpinnings of fact verification in Answer Set Programming. We examine three distinct fact verification methodologies and provide in-depth analyses of their operational mechanisms, along with their associated computational complexities. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between these methodologies and propose open questions for further investigation.

A quantum system is viewed as having resources that can be allocated and redistributed. We investigate the basic rule that defines an operation's law by examining how it affects resource distribution. We develop a framework called a universal quantum resource theory (UQRT) that considers all possible resource types simultaneously. We show that under UQRT, the law of resource-free operations corresponds to entangling operations. Furthermore, we establish UQRT for various states, operations, and structural properties.
