We develop a method for evaluating theoretical predictions using actual data. Our evaluation technique generates a metric that quantifies the discrepancy between a theoretical model and a data set for various model parameters. The evaluation curve, data plot and theoretical moment functions visually illustrate the discrepancy. The moment function's shape indicates the variability of the data, data points on the evaluation curve indicate the best possible discrepancy for various sample sizes, and points on the theoretical moment function curve represent the discrepancy for various theoretical predictions.

In this research, we explore the intertemporal relationships within multivariate time series that exhibit non-stable statistical characteristics. A novel method is introduced to identify the intertemporal dependence structure without assuming stable or subexponential distribution properties. The proposed approach relies on empirical data and theoretical findings related to the Poisson-Dirichlet distribution, which is used to order the relative importance of different time intervals. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to real-world data, specifically in the context of international stock markets, where it is shown to be more accurate than models assuming stable distributions. Additionally, the approach is shown to enable the identification of robust asset allocation strategies that can withstand non-stable and heavy-tailed market conditions.

We've developed a family of sparse parity-check matrices with low density, consisting of matrices with few non-zero entries. These matrices have a specific structure with any given row intersecting others in a specific pattern. At most half of the rows share a single non-zero entry, while the rest share no more than a single non-zero entry with any given row. These codes were initially suggested by Yehuda Bar-Natan and can be adapted to various graph types. Yehuda Bar-Natan's idea enabled the creation of efficient codes with low parity-check density and fast decoding times. We've also provided an alternative method for constructing these matrices based on a graph-based approach, where these matrices correspond to matrices derived from semi-random graphs with specific non-zero entry constraints.

In graph theory, a set of vertices is considered a distance-$r$ controlling set if every other vertex in the graph is at a distance of $r$ or less from a vertex in the set. The problem of finding the smallest distance-$r$ controlling set in a graph is generally NP-hard, but we found that when the graph is sparse and has a high order, a much smaller subset of vertices can control the distance. Specifically, we proved that a subset of vertices of size $O(n/r)$ can control the distance $r$ in any connected graph with a sparse structure, where $n$ is the total number of vertices. Furthermore, we found that vertices within distance $r$ from a randomly chosen vertex cover the graph efficiently, with high probability.

A fundamental principle in physics, known as the mass-boundary correspondence, states that a parameter that causes symmetry breaking on a boundary can also influence the bulk properties. This concept is being explored in the context of disordered one-dimensional topological insulators and superconductors, where a model is developed to examine how symmetry breaking on the boundary affects the bulk properties. The model reveals that a particular phase transition occurs when the symmetry breaking parameter reaches a critical point, and that this phase transition can be understood in terms of a localized state appearing on the boundary. The model also shows that the localized state's energy level can be controlled by adjusting the symmetry breaking parameter, and that this localized state's presence can be detected using a particular measurement technique. The model's results are consistent with those obtained using another measurement technique, known as the Landau-Bloch method, and that these results have important implications for the study of topological materials.

Recent searches for new physics at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have yielded compelling evidence for supersymmetry, particularly in meta-stable chargino/stop scenarios. Based on these findings, we have established new exclusion limits on LHC parameters for various supersymmetry models, including different stop mixing scenarios and chargino mass scenarios. Our research has significantly constrained supersymmetry parameter space, particularly in terms of stop mixing and chargino masses.

Our proposed technique, Bright Field Neural Visualization, creates transparent, see-through visualizations of data in a bright field setting by training a neural network on transparent visualization images. The resulting model can be used in a rendering pipeline to produce visibleizations, which a second neural network then corrects to remove artifacts and produce high-quality, bright field visibleizations. We evaluated our approach on five datasets and found that it successfully generates visibleizations in a bright field setting, which outperforms traditional methods.

A comprehensive analysis of the SOAR telescope's 2021 speckle program has been carried out, encompassing 40 observations of 22 targets. 11 of these targets were binary systems, 8 of which exhibited well-defined orbital paths. 10 additional targets were observed to assess the SOAR system's performance and speckle binary detection capabilities. 11 new binary star discoveries were identified, including 4 previously unknown systems. 12 previously known binary systems were also observed, with 10 showing consistent results. 102 new stellar mass estimates were calculated using co-added binary and binary + tertiary star observations. 12 new tertiary star detections were made, including 2 previously known systems. 10 tertiary mass ratios were determined, with 4 new detections of mass ratios.

We are exploring chiral algebras related to heavenly spaces in 2D and 4D super-Yang-Mills theories with super-Kahler and complexified complex geometries. These chiral algebras, formulated in terms of the Frenet frame, encompass key examples including the 2D and 4D self-dual gravity and the self-dual Wilson loop algebra. We establish an equivalence between the algebra of covariantly constant sections and the integrability of the underlying geometry. We further extend colour-kinematics duality to the covariantly constant sections, providing a computational framework for the chiral algebra. This involves constructing kinematic operators from the Lie algebra of sl(2,C) and demonstrating their action on the sections, with the operators being conserved quantities for the integrable geometries.

A comprehensive analysis of the solar flare observed on August 1, 2013, is presented, which was captured by the low-frequency radio telescope LOFAR. The analysis reveals a piston-like surge in a solar jet emanating from an active region, accompanied by distinctive radio frequency bursts known as type III bursts. Specifically, the jet's piston-like behavior was evident in the solar jet's southward progression, coinciding with the type III bursts. Radio frequency measurements taken at 145 MHz showed a growing, brightened structure, forming an arc-like shape, indicating a shock wave driven by the jet. The shock wave's characteristics, such as its speed and height, were determined to be approximately 100 km/s and 10 Mm above the solar surface, respectively. The study's analysis of the jet's piston-like behavior, along with the type III bursts, provides valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of solar jets and their associated energy release processes.

In the Standard Model, a discrepancy exists between the experimentally determined muon's anomalous magnetic moment and the value predicted by theory. This could be resolved by extending the Standard Model to include additional scalar fields. One such model is the general two Higgs doublet model, which can generate flavour-changing scalar interactions and potentially explain irregularities in lepton decays and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. Researchers have previously constrained this model's parameters using various processes, but a more comprehensive approach is necessary. In this study, we propose a new method to assess the model's validity by analyzing the probability of its parameters in different processes. Our results show that this model can be consistent with all current data, potentially explaining the observed anomalies in the LHCb's $R(D^{(*)})$ measurements and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment.

We explore a stochastic system that mimics the behavior of a whirlpool, where water particles move randomly within a confined, circular area. The motion of these particles is influenced by an external force that changes over time and a form of Brownian motion. The resulting system is a type of nonlinear equation that is difficult to solve directly, so we take an alternative approach by considering the probability distribution of the particles' positions as we increase our focus on the details of their motion as it becomes infinitely large. This approach allows us to derive a new equation that describes the system's behavior in a more tractable way. The newly derived equation is a probabilistic version of a type of nonlinear equation that arises in the study of fluid dynamics and other fields. Our work reveals that this equation accurately reflects the dynamics of the original system in a wide range of scenarios, including those where the motion of the particles is highly complex.

The state vector of a specific type of quantum sampling process, known as boson sampling, is investigated. The study reveals that the state vector of this sampling process is not entangled when the number of modes equals the number of photons, and it is fully entangled when these two values differ. The study further calculates the entanglement between any subset of modes and photons using the negativity measure. The results obtained from this calculation are then compared to those from other types of quantum sampling processes that have deterministically entangled states.

A novel approach to modeling complex temporal sequences is presented, specifically designed for efficient learning of sequence tasks. Our method involves a multi-component system that enables the discovery of sequence structure through the combination of high-capacity memory and recurrent neural networks. These networks are guided in a two-step process: first, brief sequences are used to establish a high-level understanding of task structure, and then, in a fine-tuning stage, more detailed information is used to refine the model's performance. This approach, known as Sequence Guided Learning (SGL), is demonstrated to outperform existing methods on a variety of tasks, including those found in language, mathematics, and biology. Notably, SGL achieves this improvement with significantly less training data, making it a highly efficient solution for mastering intricate temporal sequence tasks.

Recurrent neural networks, particularly when used in partially observable environments, have a natural connection to agents that form beliefs about their hidden states. A specific subset of these networks, called concealed state networks, can efficiently represent accurate beliefs even in challenging environments. However, it has been proven that most recurrent networks operating in partially observable environments cannot consistently maintain up-to-date beliefs. In response to this limitation, a new class of recurrent networks has been developed, which can reliably represent beliefs in any partial Markov decision process, provided the network size is sufficiently large, which is polynomial in nature.

This paper introduces an innovative weakly-supervised machine learning framework for detecting actions in videos. Unlike existing weakly-supervised methods, our proposed framework leverages visual cues to identify key contextual information in videos. We introduce a novel graph-based approach for context learning using graph convolutional networks, which can be trained with minimal human annotations. To achieve this, we design a novel graph data structure that represents the relationships between detected action instances, which can be learned using GCNs. Furthermore, we introduce a new loss function for video classification that builds upon graph-level predictions. Extensive experiments conducted on the Kinetics-400 and Kinetics673-1000 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, which significantly outperforms state-of-the-art weakly-supervised methods.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge brought together a group of researchers to compare and contrast state-of-the-art methods for detecting local image similarities. Held as part of the 10th IEEE International Conference on Image Formation and Electronics, the challenge focused on evaluating methods for detecting image overlaps and novel views. Following a successful first edition in 2020, the challenge aimed to address the limitations of traditional methods in handling large overlaps and novel views better. Out of the 40 submissions received, the challenge saw significant advancements in overlap detection, with the winning approach achieving impressive results, boasting 98.5% accuracy on the test set. The winning method, dubbed "MegaNet," demonstrated remarkable resilience, with the top five approaches achieving overlap accuracy above 95%. The challenge also saw promising results on the novel view task, with the winning approach achieving 80.5% accuracy, surpassing the performance of the previous year. The challenge's success underscores the importance of diverse and robust datasets in advancing the field of image similarity detection.

This text explores the long-term behavior of solutions in parabolic partial differential equations that feature degenerating coefficients, specifically focusing on boundary disturbances and their connection to metastable states. The given boundary problems can be seen as mathematical representations of underlying physical phenomena, such as phase transitions in alloys, where the parameters in these equations have clear physical interpretations. Consequently, understanding the asymptotic behavior of the solutions is crucial for analyzing the observed phenomena. Additionally, we will investigate the homogenization of parabolic equations when the coefficients become increasingly degenerate, with the ultimate goal of understanding the emergence of sharp interface models that describe metastable states.

The correlation energy of nuclear substance under a strong magnetic field is calculated using the local orbital correlated vector model. This model incorporates correlated Fermi gas, related to the correlated vector model. We consider the effect of a strong magnetic field on the correlation energy, and calculate it using the LOCV method with the Argonne $v_{14}$ potential. We also calculate the effect of a strong magnetic field on the root-mean-square radius of the nucleon distribution.

Achieving secure communication in Federated Learning (FL) is crucial for safeguarding sensitive user data and maintaining user privacy. To balance communication efficiency and data confidentiality, we introduce a new framework, called Differential Privacy Communication (DPC), which optimizes both objectives. Our framework leverages differential privacy to create secure communication channels, and it offers a comprehensive analysis of its accuracy and confidentiality properties. We also develop a distributed algorithm to efficiently generate secure noise for the DPC framework. Through theoretical and experimental evaluations, the proposed approach, called REC, demonstrates its potential to significantly reduce communication overhead while ensuring accurate model training and robust user privacy protection.

A research team has conducted far-ultraviolet observations of the Taurus-Auriga star-forming region using the FUSE telescope, focusing on the ACO-SF-R1 cloud. The study aims to map molecular hydrogen emissions, specifically H2, in this area, which is shrouded in dust and thus difficult to observe in other wavelengths. The team's results show that H2 emissions are primarily located at the edges of the dust-shrouded clouds, where they are illuminated by nearby O and B stars, and that these regions coincide with areas of molecular hydrogen excitation. The study also found that H2 emissions are not limited to the edges of the clouds, but are also found in some central regions, which may be due to the presence of smaller dust grains or a different physical process. The research provides new insights into the physical processes that occur in star-forming regions and the excitation mechanisms of molecular hydrogen.

Structured tabular data, presented in tables, effectively condenses vast amounts of information, making it a crucial component of written language. The efficient representation of this data format is vital, as it can significantly impact data comprehension. Recent advancements in machine learning have led to the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in table representation tasks, leveraging the natural correspondence between GNNs and table structures. Despite the potential of GNNs, research into table representation remains limited, with a need for further exploration. This paper introduces a novel approach to table representation through the integration of GNNs and a novel representation encoding method called Table Structure Graph (TSG). The proposed TSG method involves a detailed analysis of table structures, while the selection of a suitable GNN architecture is a key component of the approach. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in various table representation tasks.

We introduce a comprehensive model of strategic interactions that incorporates multiple stages of decision-making under information insufficiency. At each stage, agents form expectations about the actions of others, leading to a sequence of beliefs and strategies that converge to an equilibrium. In each round, agents assess their information and anticipate how other agents will use this shared information, leading to a progressive deepening of understanding. Our model is applied to analyze dynamic games of incomplete information, including entry deterrence in oligopolies, and we also investigate how increasing information precision affects outcomes in a specific game scenario.

In the absence of reliable census data, autonomous survey models estimate population counts to produce accurate size estimates for enumeration. This method is particularly beneficial for developing nations, as seen in Mozambique, where our team has been working to establish a sustainable autonomous survey system. The main obstacle to implementing this model in Mozambique has been the lack of suitable hardware, as local government agencies have not been able to afford specialized devices capable of processing complex statistical models. To address this issue, we have been exploring the use of more affordable hardware platforms, such as the Raspberry Pi, to facilitate accurate and efficient size estimation based on survey sample designs.

The challenge of efficiently managing large collections of data, such as databases, arises from the need to address the following issues: (a) quickly determining if a piece of data belongs to the collection, and (b) quickly locating and retrieving that data when applicable. To address this issue, researchers have developed data structures known as membership query filters (MQF), which can quickly determine whether a piece of data belongs to a collection. However, traditional MQFs have a drawback: they can incorrectly claim that some data belongs to a collection when it does not. To overcome this issue, we have developed a novel framework for creating an exact filter that guarantees no false claims. This framework involves taking an existing, possibly inaccurate filter and processing it to remove all errors. The main contribution of this work is the demonstration that our method can transform any existing, possibly inaccurate filter into an exact filter while maintaining a reasonable size and performance. Theoretically, our method guarantees no false claims, and it can be applied to a variety of different filters. The method has been tested using various types of filters, and it has been shown to outperform other methods in terms of efficiency and storage requirements.

We investigate a BCS-BEC crossover in the context of atom-molecule duality, specifically in systems involving spin-1/2 atoms and bosonic diatomic molecules. Our analysis centers on a laser-induced manipulation of the spin-1/2 atoms, transforming them into spinor molecules with a specific total spin configuration. The driving force behind this transformation is a spin-dependent recombination process, modeled as a contact interaction with a tunable interaction strength. Our findings reveal that under this interaction, BCS-like atoms can be converted into BEC-like molecules, and we calculate the critical parameters necessary to achieve this conversion. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of experimentally observing this process, and we discuss the implications of our results for realizing spinor atom-molecule duality.

A novel approach to fluid-structure interaction problems, particularly in cases involving multiple scales, is developed and tested using the material point method. The method integrates an immersed boundary approach to enforce boundary conditions and the level set method to distinguish between fluids and solids, thereby enabling accurate simulation of complex flows, such as those involving bubbles and droplets. The resulting framework demonstrates its effectiveness in a variety of test cases, such as the movement of a single bubble near a solid boundary, the interaction between a liquid jet and a solid target, and the complex dynamics of a liquid droplet impacting a solid surface.

A quantum machine learning model that operates independently of feedback has shown promising results in various fields, including physics, biology, and finance. Despite its promise, monitoring quantum data requires a large amount of resources, which can be prohibitive in current quantum devices. We've developed a new approach to improve this situation by incorporating feedback into the learning process. We've used a superconducting quantum processor to implement this method in a study involving synthetic data, which has been generated using two different approaches. We've also investigated the impact of varying the number of quantum and classical parameters on the model's performance. We've discovered that adding feedback to the learning process can improve its efficiency, especially in complex data sets. We've also observed that a hybrid learning approach, which combines classical and quantum methods, can be more effective in certain applications.

A recently developed neural network, FastPitch, has the ability to generate speech 
by controlling pitch. However, it's been found that some training samples with 
similar pitch patterns can lead to less controlled speech generation. To address 
this issue, we have created an augmentation technique that expands the pitch 
range without affecting the original speech characteristics. When used with 
FastPitch, our approach allows for more controlled speech generation and also 
retains the original timbre.

The growing interest in modeling the dynamic behavior of cities has led to the development of numerous approaches for accurate predictions of traffic patterns. However, existing models struggle to effectively handle complex, multi-hop relationships and spatial-temporal data, which are essential for understanding city dynamics. This research introduces Hopper, a novel deep learning framework designed to tackle the limitations of current approaches. Hopper leverages a hierarchical graph to model multi-hop relationships and a specialized attention mechanism to capture spatial and temporal dependencies. Through comprehensive evaluations on two large-scale datasets, Hopper demonstrates superior performance in modeling city dynamics, particularly in accurate predictions of traffic patterns.

The W boson mass is a crucial parameter, and its precise measurement is a key objective.
This measurement is carried out using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider.
Data collected from proton-proton collisions at an energy of 13 TeV with a total of 36.1 fb^-1 of luminosity are analyzed.
The lepton mass scale is determined through the pp -> W/Z + b\bar{b} production process.
The results are presented for two decay modes of the W boson: electrons and muons.
In the electrons case, the Z boson mass is determined to be 91.09 +/- 0.75 (statistical) +/- 1.05 (systematic) GeV.
For the muons, the Z boson mass is determined to be 91.42 +/- 0.13 (statistical) +/- 0.73 (systematic) GeV.
These results are in agreement with the world average.
Additionally, the W boson mass is determined to be 80.31 +/- 0.12 (statistical) +/- 0.16 (systematic) GeV for the muons and 80.36 +/- 0.14 (statistical) +/- 0.16 (systematic) GeV for the electrons case.

This study introduces an innovative evaluation method for Telepresence Robot (TR) quality of experience (QoE) by focusing on the remote user's (RU) ability to navigate the TR in a real-world setting. By conducting an interactive evaluation, we gather RUs' feedback on their robot control quality through a 20-meter indoor navigation task. We assess three QoE factors - navigation ease, trust in the TR, and perceived control quality - via surveys distributed to RUs. Additionally, we investigate the correlation between these QoE factors and RUs' performance metrics, including time taken to complete the navigation task and collision frequency. The results reveal that the You Drive Me Insane (YDMI) evaluation method is a promising tool for evaluating TR QoE, outperforming conventional approaches.

This study introduces hierarchical linear regression models, also referred to as multilevel models, from a Bayesian viewpoint. We demonstrate how Bayesian multilevel models can be derived from a common set of assumptions, and how these models can be solved using a singular algebraic approach, rather than the conventional MCMC method. This singular approach is simpler and more efficient than MCMC, particularly for large datasets, and our findings are illustrated through a case study involving a study on the determinants of students' academic achievement.

The game of Mafia, also known as Murder, has gained significant popularity in party settings. We utilize a simulation model to analyze various gameplay strategies. Our model reveals that in games with no experience, Mafia players tend to outlast their civilian counterparts. However, as the game progresses and the proportion of Mafia players increases, the advantage shifts to civilians. Introducing experience into the game significantly increases the likelihood of Mafia players winning. Additionally, our model explores the impact of two specific Mafia strategies: shooting and voting. It is discovered that the strategy of voting is more effective than shooting, and that Mafia players can improve their chances of winning by selectively targeting individuals who are less likely to vote, such as those with a history of not voting or showing signs of being a civilian.

The formation of super-Earths and mini-Neptunes is a significant process in planetary systems. To understand this, we studied how two large planets form and impact the surrounding disk. Using a sophisticated computer model, we simulated the formation of these planets and found that when two massive planets form simultaneously, they significantly affect the surrounding disk. This effect is more pronounced when the planets are close to each other. As a result, the disk's gas distribution changes, which can lead to variations in the final mass of the planets and even cause smaller planets to form elsewhere. This effect is more pronounced when the planets are close to each other. Our study shows that the formation of these planets is a complex process that depends on the interactions between the planets and the surrounding disk.

A novel electronic energy transfer mechanism has been discovered in carbon nanotube clusters, where scissor phonons facilitate the transfer process. This discovery challenges the long-held assumption that a phonon-mediated energy transfer mechanism is inefficient. In contrast to the previously believed mechanism, our research reveals that the interplay between electronic and phonon modes in graphene-based systems can lead to a highly efficient energy transfer mechanism. This mechanism is driven by a phonon-assisted process that significantly reduces the energy transfer rate. Our research demonstrates that the phonon-assisted mechanism can dominate over a previously believed mechanism, providing a new understanding of energy transfer in carbon nanotube clusters.

This article introduces a novel fuzzy k-means clustering approach, referred to as VFKMC, which addresses a crucial aspect in high-dimensional data analysis - the varying relevance of features. Unlike conventional k-means methods, VFKMC assigns each data point to one cluster unambiguously and determines a unique data-based feature weight vector, thereby minimizing entropy within each cluster. The VFKMC method is proven to converge, and a comprehensive analysis explores its optimal convergence under an ideal scenario. Furthermore, the paper showcases the efficacy of VFKMC through several numerical examples, highlighting its ability to outperform traditional methods in clustering high-dimensional data.

Mixture-of-Experts, a widely used machine learning model, has seen significant advancements in recent years, particularly the development of stochastic third-order algorithms for the general non-convex non-convex setting. These algorithms, however, come with a substantial computational cost due to their third-order gradient calculations. Our work introduces a group-based gradient aggregation technique that enables a distributed implementation of these algorithms, achieving a notable reduction in complexity. The theoretical analysis supports this improvement, demonstrating a notable enhancement in both the algorithm's reliability and efficiency, especially in handling scenarios involving convex and non-convex data. This breakthrough surpasses existing theoretical advancements in the field, establishing new benchmarks for Mixture-of-Experts model optimization.

We examine a class of loop games played on bipartite graphs that build upon the well-known token-firing and discrete harmonic functions. Our study reveals a Jacobi-Liouville correspondence connecting the spectral properties of a quotient Jacobian to a compact Riemann surface, derived from the graph's quotient under a natural involution. This correspondence is used to establish a complete set of conditions for a loop game to be equivalent to the chip-firing game on the resulting Riemann surface.

The observation of primordial gravitational waves via their induced birefringence in the Cosmic B-mode signal holds great promise for probing quantum gravity. We suggest that any disruption of a global symmetry in quantum gravity will inevitably lead to the production of pseudoscalar particles, the decay of which generates birefringence. We argue that disrupting a global symmetry in quantum gravity is unfeasible, and therefore, any observed disruption must be an artifact of our current understanding. We then derive a constraint on the scale at which a given global symmetry could potentially be broken, based on the birefringence data. We apply this reasoning to several examples, including the $U(1)$ symmetry in string theory and a hypothetical $SO(3)$ symmetry in gravity. We also explore the possibility that the birefringence arises from couplings between pseudoscalar fields and curvature, and discuss the implications of our findings.

By analyzing the cluster's color-magnitude diagram, researchers found a distinct blue horizontal branch (BHB) and a red horizontal branch (RHB) with a blue and a red turn-off, respectively. A unique feature in the BHB region was discovered, indicating the presence of a group of stars with blue horizontal branch (BHB) characteristics.
